extracted.intended_audience: general readers, media fans, and creators looking for examples and techniques for humorous/gag credits across TV, film, radio, music, games, and liner notes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for creating humorous, novelty, or parody credits/liner notes across media (television, film, radio, music, games), covering techniques like punny names, interrupted credits, altered styles, fake roles, and meta-jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punny Name / Faux-name credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace real names with punny, homophonic, or joke names (often labelled 'Punny Name').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Strictly Come Dancing giving punny names for Halloween, MAD #2 replacing artists' first names with 'Melvin', Camper Van Beethoven using Lemony-Narrator asides, The Queen Is Dead crediting 'Ann Coates' (a pun on Ancoats). Used widely in TV, music liner notes, and comedy shows to elicit a quick laugh or inside joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform-name gag
rubrics_metrics.description: Give every credited person the same first name (or other identical label) to extend a running gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Price Is Right April Fools episode — every contestant wore a nametag saying 'Pat' and closing credits changed everyone's first name to Pat. Keeps the gag consistent through credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diegetic interruption of credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Have on-screen action interrupt, cover, or refuse the credits (characters prevent or interact with the credits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: She Spies — Cassie swallows a bomb and refuses to allow the credits to run; WandaVision — Wanda literally rolls the credits over the show to end an argument but Vision refuses to stop them. Use to continue the joke into or through the credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits in alternate language or musical style
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the theme or credits sung/voiced in a different language or musical genre to match episode conceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Psych theme sung in Spanish; Bollywood-style musical episode with Hindi credits; theme sung by Boyz II Men; Elvis-style or Hammond-organ versions. Effective for genre parodies or themed episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pause credits for character commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Pause or freeze the credits to allow a character to comment, prolong a joke, or break the fourth wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Red Dwarf paused the credits in 'Waiting For God' so Rimmer could wail about the episode's reveal. Good for letting a character 'talk over' the credits for comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirrored / reversed / backward credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Run the credits as a mirror image, backwards, or in reverse order as a visual gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Remastered 'Backwards' with credits as a mirror image; album tracklists listed in reverse order (Hot Hot Heat's Elevator). Creates disorientation or ties into episode/album concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truncated or first-name-only credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit people by only their first name (or an abbreviated name) for comedic or stylistic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Roseanne — after a cast/crediting change, every credit was shown as just the person's first name. Can feel intimate, irreverent, or emphasize a performer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altered order / punctuation for gag
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the usual ordering or add punctuation to names/titles to create a joke (e.g., question marks, non-alphabetical order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SNL season finale where question marks follow every name; SNL episode with non-alphabetical cast ordering as part of the conceit. Ordering and punctuation can be used to parody seriousness or create suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoofed-title / style-of-other-work credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Design opening/closing credits to parody or mimic the style of another work or director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SNL spoofing Planet of the Apes; Twin Peaks tribute with original artist performing an extended version; Francis Ford Coppola-styled opening. Useful for affectionate parody or intertextual humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relocated credits (start vs end) or unexpected placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Place credits at the start, in the middle, or otherwise not at the conventional moment to subvert expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Screenwipe ran the credits at the start, then cut to a spoof documentary, later remarking they had already been shown. Moving credits can be used for meta-commentary or to set up a gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake end credits and made-up crew names
rubrics_metrics.description: Run fake end credits populated with invented crew names, fictional roles, or gag contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: WandaVision includes fake end credits with made-up crew names; Screenwipe and many comedy shows use fake credits to extend satire. Useful for worldbuilding or continuing the joke past runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous job titles / role descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: List contributors with silly, unexpected, or absurd role names instead of standard credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pat Sajak as 'Pumpkin Picker'; Adam McKay as 'director of falconry'; Rush album dedications like 'world-renowned they'. Often used for comic character-building or to lampoon industry conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsensical 'thanks' and irreverent acknowledgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill liner notes or 'thanks' sections with jokes, snipes, or intentionally absurd acknowledgements (including negative thank-yous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NOFX 'No thanx' list, Pavement's 'All Wrongs Reversed', Five Iron Frenzy's nonsense thank-yous. Can convey band personality or poke fun at industry/expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate misattribution / wrong instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally credit the wrong instrument, list incorrect contributors, or swap roles as a gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jello Biafra collaboration crediting wrong instruments; Pigface/NIN songwriting credit dispute and its humorous responses. Works as playful deception or a pointed commentary on credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit non-human contributors (software, animals, objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit software, pets, or inanimate objects as performers or contributors for comic effect or commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vane Lily video credits software used for vocals; Zappa album credits dogs as musicians. Can be used to joke about production quirks or personnel changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonyms and insider-aliases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pseudonyms, alter-egos, or inside-reference aliases (e.g., Dale Nixon, Fluss) to credit contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Steve Albini credited as his cat Fluss; Greg Ginn's 'Dale Nixon' pseudonym tradition. Pseudonyms can hide identities humorously or reference subcultural in-jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful legal / disclaimer gags
rubrics_metrics.description: Subvert standard legal language or disclaimers for humor (e.g., twist 'All Rights Reserved').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pavement's 'All Wrongs Reversed', Tubular Bells stereo/mono joke. Such gags appear in liner notes or packaging copy to surprise readers used to boilerplate text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liner notes formatted as other genres or devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure liner notes/credits as a different genre (e.g., a book blurb, recipe, product box copy) to extend a concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: That dog.'s track-list written like a blurb for a teen novel; Michael Nesmith's liner notes as a homemade beer recipe. Reinforces album concept or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits used as narrative device or teaser
rubrics_metrics.description: Make credits part of narrative teasing (cliffhanger parody) or to announce future events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: SNL's 'Who Will Survive? Who Will Perish?' captions preceding credits as a cliffhanger parody. Credits can be integrated into storytelling or marketing jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits recited in verse, limerick, or poetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Render the credits as verse, limerick, or another poetic form instead of a list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John Finnemore's Souvenir Programme had credits read as insults or a limerick; Hitchhiker's Guide closing credits with repetitive 'I only happened to be...' lines. Adds a literary or comedic flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit anagrams and wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform production names into anagrams or other wordplay for the end credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ask Me Another features the puzzle guru turning production names into anagrams. Wordplay entertains attentive viewers and rewards repeat listening/viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shout-outs, inside-references, and cultural callbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill credits/liner notes with pop-culture references, shout-outs to other works, or in-jokes aimed at a savvy audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Melvins' 'A. Hilter' as a Monty Python shout-out; many albums credit fictional groups or refer to prior sketches. Builds rapport with fans who catch references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake endorsements and parody product mentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include mock instrument endorsements, product-claim jokes, or spoof corporate copy in credits/liner notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luscious Jackson instrument 'endorsements', NOFX spoofing endorsements ('NOFX used guitars, drums... and other stuff too'). Good for satire of commercialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive or secret-mode credits (games/pinball)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hide special credits behind secret inputs or show special credit sequences in attract modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stern's Pirates of the Caribbean attract mode showing developers as pirates via secret flipper combination; RoboCop pinball listing 'The Cybernetic Love Commandos.' Useful to reward players and add developer humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual-prop gags in credit text
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify credit typography or decorate text with seasonal/prop elements (snow, Santa hats, candy canes, replaced letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Psych Christmas episodes with fake snow and props replacing letters; closing credits with Santa hats. Visual tweaks reinforce seasonal jokes or episode themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal trivia or irrelevant details in credits
rubrics_metrics.description: List irrelevant personal details (shoe size, astrological sign, favorite foods) alongside standard credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Flaming Lips listing shoe size/astrological sign; Wire listing a physical feature per member. Adds personality and small, amusing surprises for fans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits as satire of broadcasting or production policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the credits to critique or lampoon broadcaster rules or production norms (meta-commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Charlie Brooker's Screenwipe pokes fun at BBC policy of not having anything happening in end credits by running them early and commenting on them. Works as institutional satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits extending sketch performance or audience participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the reading/format of the credits itself a performative element (cast reads credits in-character or audience is credited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Whose Line Is It Anyway? has the winning performer read credits in a chosen style; Five Iron Frenzy included audience members' names as 'backing vocals' from sign-up sheets. Makes credits participatory or performative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate factual inaccuracy for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Give intentionally wrong factual data in credits/liner notes (wrong track lengths, incorrect locations, fictional biographical details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grammatrain listing odd track lengths like 4:71; Camper Van Beethoven's whimsical sleeve copy and false details. Used to unsettle expectations and add absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themed group-labeling of contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace normal credits with themed group labels (e.g., 'Latino All Stars', 'R. C. singer-songwriter') to fit a conceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Havalina Rail Co. referring to guest musicians as 'Latino All Stars'; many specials listing everyone as 'Sir Ranulph (surname)' or 'Björn (surname)'. Reinforces episode or special theme and can be used to lampoon formality.
